expert: Hi, Skyler! Is this a new plant? If so, do you know what the cultivar it is? I found a cultivar, Taxus Baccata, that the new growth is yellow.  Taxus (Anglo-Japanese Yew, English Yew, Japanese Yew, Pacific Yew, Western Yew, Yew) | North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox (ncsu.edu)  Please let me know the cultivar so I can do more research.

Just trying to figure out if the problem is nutritional or possibly pathogen or insect related. It would be helpful to know if this is a localized problem or possibly occurring in other locals. My first thought would be to add some iron either granular fertilizer or a liquid spray. user: Hello, I found two of these odd structures in our lawn near our evergreen trees and would like an opinion as to what it is.  It appears to be some kind of bag worm or insect sac since larvae can be seen.  We have two Ponderosa pines, a Fat Albert Spruce and a Douglas fir in the back yard.   Thank you.
expert: Hello, Drew. White, Unusual indeed! The parts of insects on the outside of the mass are mealworms (larvae of darkling beetles). These insects are rarely plant pests, and they certainly do not attack evergreen trees.  What you have observed is a bird’s regurgitation pellet. Akin to the better-known owl pellets, some songbirds regurgitate pellets comprised of insect exoskeletons and other byproducts of feeding. The large size and abundance of mealworm exuviae can be explained by backyard bird feeding, as many people put out mealworms now to feed birds over the winter. There appear to be kernels and fragments of grains in the mass, which are also components of backyard feeders.

user: my grapevines have these enlarged "nodes" on the stems. (Never seen this before over 20 years.). Some leaves are deformed with growths, holes, and few are withered. No fruit, but never had grapes in the past.

This is a very old grape vine that runs 40 feet along a fence. Some sections don't seem to have this problem. other section have a lot and bigger swollen stem "nodes".

I live in the Como area of Saint Paul.  Thank you.
expert: These two phenomena are unrelated. The leaves are being attacked by an insect with chewing mouth parts.  Grape beetles are the likely suspect but there are other possibilities.  Try to get a picture of them and we can more accurately identify the insect. See:  https://extension.umn.edu/yard-and-garden-insects/scarab-beetles  The nodes on the vines are normal.  They are called lateral buds and contain the next year’s vines and leaves.  See:  https://extension.umn.edu/fruit/growing-grapes-home-garden

user: Innovation zoysia put down in July 2022.  Was terrible last spring after winter kill but did well by July-Sept.  Now it has what I wonder is fungus.  I put down fungicide Lebanon Eagle 0.62 in late March and repeated 2 weeks later.  Does not seem to be helping much.  Advice?  Thanks.
expert: It is normal for your Zoysia lawn to look tan and dry right now. Zoysia is a different type of grass than what is the recommended and commonly used grasses for lawns in most of Maryland, which is turf-type tall fescue. Most lawn grasses here are what are termed 'cool season' grasses. They green up and start to grow early in the spring. In the hottest part of summer, when we lack rain, it slows down and is best allowed to go dormant, but it will green up again once there is rain and cooler weather.  Zoysia, on the other hand, is a southern 'warm-season' grass. It doesn't  turn green and start growing again until well into May.  Here is our page on Zoysia lawns and their care:  https://extension.umd.edu/resource/planting-and-maintaining-zoysia-lawn/   Christine
